questions.stem: In the Standard Model, which gauge boson carries the electromagnetic force?
options: The W boson
The Z boson
The photon
The gluon
questions.explanation: Gauge bosons are the force-carrying particles. Photons carry the electromagnetic force, gluons the strong force, and W and Z bosons the weak force.

questions.stem: Which gauge bosons carry the strong force?
options: Gluons
Photons
W and Z bosons
Neutrinos
questions.explanation: Gluons carry the strong force between quarks, which have colour charge. Photons carry the electromagnetic force and W and Z bosons the weak force. Neutrinos are not gauge bosons at all.

questions.stem: Which gauge bosons carry the weak force?
options: Photons
Up and down quarks
W and Z bosons
Gluons
questions.explanation: The weak force is carried by the W and Z bosons. Up and down quarks are matter particles that make up protons and neutrons, not force carriers.

questions.stem: A neutron in a nucleus changes into a proton, and an electron is emitted. Which force, and which gauge boson, is responsible?
options: The weak force, carried by a W boson
The strong force, carried by a gluon
The electromagnetic force, carried by a photon
The weak force, carried by a gluon
questions.explanation: Beta-minus decay changes a down quark into an up quark, turning a neutron into a proton. Changing the type of a quark is the work of the weak force, carried by a W boson. Gluons hold quarks together but do not change their type.

questions.stem: What does it mean to say that a gauge boson carries a force?
options: It stores the energy of a force until a collision releases it
Particles interact by exchanging it, and the exchange produces the force
It is a particle that is pushed by the force more than any other
It is a particle that has no mass and never interacts with matter
questions.explanation: In the Standard Model, forces arise when particles exchange gauge bosons. Two charged particles, for example, interact by exchanging photons. Not all gauge bosons are massless: the W and Z bosons have mass.

questions.stem: What holds the quarks inside a proton together?
options: Gravity, which is very strong at the tiny distances inside a proton
The strong force, carried by gluons acting on the quarks' colour charge
The electromagnetic force, carried by photons acting on the quarks' electric charge
The weak force, carried by W and Z bosons acting between the quarks
questions.explanation: Quarks carry colour charge, and the strong force between colour charges is carried by gluons. The electromagnetic force could not do it: a proton's two up quarks both have positive charge and repel each other electrically.

questions.stem: An electron is held in orbit around a hydrogen nucleus. In Standard Model terms, which gauge boson is exchanged between the electron and the proton?
options: The W boson
The Z boson
The photon
The gluon
questions.explanation: The attraction between the negative electron and the positive proton is electromagnetic, carried by photons. The electron has no colour charge, so gluons play no part, and the weak force does not bind atoms.

questions.stem: Which fundamental interaction is not described by the Standard Model's gauge bosons?
options: The strong force
The weak force
The electromagnetic force
Gravity
questions.explanation: The Standard Model's gauge bosons cover three interactions: the strong force (gluons), the weak force (W and Z bosons) and electromagnetism (photons). Gravity is described by general relativity and is not part of the Standard Model.

questions.stem: When do the predictions of special relativity differ significantly from those of Newtonian physics?
options: When objects are very massive, such as planets and stars
When objects accelerate quickly, as a car does from rest
When objects are very small, such as atoms and electrons
When objects move at speeds approaching the speed of light
questions.explanation: Special relativity and Newtonian physics agree closely at everyday speeds. The differences become significant only as speeds approach c. Very small objects are the domain of quantum physics, a different departure from classical ideas.

questions.stem: Muons are created high in the atmosphere by cosmic rays and travel towards the ground at nearly the speed of light. Which observation cannot be explained by Newtonian physics?
options: Muons are deflected by Earth's magnetic field as they travel downward
Muons lose a little energy as they pass through the air
Muons are created only when cosmic rays strike molecules in the air
Far more muons reach the ground than their half-life should allow
questions.explanation: Even at nearly c, the trip takes many muon half-lives by Earth clocks, so Newtonian physics predicts that very few should survive. Many more are detected at the ground. Magnetic deflection and energy loss are explained without relativity.

questions.stem: From the point of view of an observer on the ground, why do so many high-speed muons reach Earth's surface?
options: The atmosphere is length-contracted, so the ground observer sees a shorter trip
The muons travel faster than light, so they arrive before they can decay
The muons gain energy from the air, which extends their lifetime
The muons' half-life is dilated: their internal clocks run slow as seen from the ground
questions.explanation: In the ground frame the muons move at nearly c, so their decay process is observed to run slow; their half-life is dilated and more survive the trip. The ground observer sees the atmosphere at its normal thickness. Nothing with mass can travel faster than light.

questions.stem: Seen from the muon's own frame of reference, the muon's half-life is normal. How does a muon's frame explain why it reaches the ground?
options: The ground moves towards the muon faster than light, so it arrives in time
The muon decays as normal, but its decay products reach the ground instead
The atmosphere rushing past is contracted, so the trip is shorter
The muon's clock runs slow, so its half-life is dilated in its own frame
questions.explanation: In its own frame the muon is at rest and its clock runs normally. Instead, the atmosphere moves past at nearly c and is contracted along the direction of motion, so the ground arrives before many half-lives have passed. Both frames agree on how many muons survive.

questions.stem: In a particle accelerator, protons are given more and more energy. What happens as their speed approaches the speed of light?
options: Their momentum stops increasing once their speed reaches half the speed of light
Their speed eventually exceeds c if enough energy is supplied
Their momentum keeps increasing, but their speed increases less and less
Their speed increases in proportion to the energy added
questions.explanation: Relativistic momentum increases without limit as the speed approaches c, so each addition of energy raises the momentum a lot but the speed only slightly. Newtonian physics would predict the speed rising steadily past c, which is never observed.

questions.stem: What is the first postulate of Einstein's special theory of relativity?
options: Nothing with mass can travel faster than the speed of light
All inertial frames are equivalent: physical laws are the same in each
The speed of light in a vacuum is the same for every inertial observer
Mass and energy are equivalent, and are related by the equation E = mc²
questions.explanation: The first postulate says no inertial frame is special: the laws of physics take the same form in all of them. The constancy of the speed of light is the second postulate. Mass-energy equivalence and the speed limit are consequences of the theory, not its postulates.

questions.stem: What is the second postulate of special relativity?
options: The speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers
The speed of light depends on the speed of the source emitting it
Time passes at the same rate for all observers, whatever their motion through space
Light needs a medium, the aether, through which to travel
questions.explanation: The second postulate is that the speed of light in a vacuum, c, is an absolute constant, measured to be the same by every inertial observer regardless of the motion of the source or the observer. Absolute time is the Newtonian idea that relativity replaced.

questions.stem: What is an inertial frame of reference?
options: A frame that is rotating steadily
A frame that accelerates uniformly
A frame moving at the speed of light
A frame that is not accelerating
questions.explanation: An inertial frame is one in which Newton's first law holds, so it is either at rest or moving at constant velocity. Rotating and accelerating frames are non-inertial, and no frame of reference can move at the speed of light.

questions.stem: A spaceship travelling towards Earth at half the speed of light switches on a forward-pointing beam. What speed does an observer on Earth measure for the light in the beam?
options: Slightly less than 1.5c
c
questions.explanation: By the second postulate, every inertial observer measures light in a vacuum travelling at c, regardless of the motion of the source. Adding the speeds, as Newtonian physics would, gives 1.5c, which is never observed.

questions.stem: A passenger in a closed train carriage moving at a constant velocity on a perfectly smooth track does experiments with pendulums and springs. Can these tell her whether the carriage is moving?
options: No, because the laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame
Yes, because a pendulum swings more slowly when it is moving
Yes, because springs stretch further in the direction of motion
No, but only because the effects are too small to measure
questions.explanation: The first postulate says all inertial frames are equivalent, so no experiment done inside the carriage can reveal its constant velocity. The results would be identical at rest. This is a statement of principle, not a limit on how precise the measurements are.

questions.stem: A spacecraft moving away from Earth at 0.6c sends a light signal back towards Earth. At what speed does the signal travel, as measured by an observer on the spacecraft and by one on Earth?
options: 0.4c for both observers
c for both observers
c on the spacecraft and 0.4c on Earth
1.6c on the spacecraft and c on Earth
questions.explanation: The second postulate applies to every inertial observer: each measures light in a vacuum moving at c. Subtracting 0.6c from c, as Newtonian velocity addition would, gives 0.4c, but that is not what is measured.

questions.stem: Newtonian physics treats length and time as absolute. How does special relativity treat them?
options: As absolute quantities, the same for every observer
As absolute for time, but relative for length and distance
As relative, but only for observers who are accelerating
As relative quantities that depend on the observer's frame
questions.explanation: Relativity shows that motion can only be measured relative to an observer, and that the length of an object and the time between two events depend on the observer's frame. Both change, and the effects apply between inertial frames.

questions.stem: An observer watches a clock that is moving past at a speed close to c. How does the moving clock appear to run, compared with the observer's own clock?
options: Backwards
Slower
Faster
At the same rate
questions.explanation: This is time dilation: a clock moving relative to an observer is measured to run slow compared with clocks at rest in the observer's frame. The effect grows as the relative speed approaches c.

questions.stem: An astronaut travels at a speed close to c relative to Earth. How does the astronaut experience the passing of time on board?
options: Normally: clocks, heartbeat and ageing all seem ordinary on board
Slowly: the astronaut notices clocks on board running slow
Quickly: the astronaut notices clocks on board running fast
Not at all: time stops for objects moving near c
questions.explanation: In the astronaut's own frame, everything on board happens at the normal rate. It is an observer on Earth who measures the ship's clocks running slow. Time dilation is a difference between frames, not something felt on board.

questions.stem: What is proper time?
options: The time between two events in the frame where both happen at the same place
The time between two events measured by an observer at rest on Earth
The time between two events measured by the fastest-moving observer
The time that light takes to travel between the places where two events happen
questions.explanation: Proper time is measured in the frame where both events occur at the same place, for example by a clock carried by a muon from its creation to its decay. Every other observer measures a longer, dilated time between the same two events.

questions.stem: Two spaceships pass each other at a high constant relative speed. Each crew watches the other ship's clocks. What do they observe?
options: Each crew sees the other ship's clocks running slow
Both crews agree that the faster ship's clocks run slow
Each crew sees the other ship's clocks running fast
Neither sees any difference, since both are moving
questions.explanation: By the first postulate, neither inertial frame is special, so the effect is symmetric: each crew measures the other's clocks running slow. Both are correct in their own frames. There is no absolute way to say which ship is really moving.

questions.stem: Why do we never notice time dilation or length contraction in everyday life?
options: The effects only happen in a vacuum, not in air
The effects only apply to light and subatomic particles, not to everyday objects
Earth's gravity cancels the effects for objects near its surface
Everyday speeds are tiny compared with c, so the effects are far too small to notice
questions.explanation: The effects depend on how close the speed is to c. Even a jet aircraft travels at less than a millionth of c, so the differences are far below anything we could notice, though precise atomic clocks can detect them. The effects apply to all objects.

questions.stem: A spaceship flies past Earth at a speed close to c. In which direction does an observer on Earth measure the ship to be contracted?
options: Only perpendicular to its direction of motion
Equally in all directions
In no direction, since only time is affected
Only along its direction of motion
questions.explanation: Length contraction happens only along the direction of relative motion. The ship's width and height, perpendicular to its motion, are measured to be unchanged.

questions.stem: What is the proper length of an object?
options: Its length measured by an observer moving at the speed of light
Its length measured by any observer on Earth
The shortest length any observer could measure for it
Its length measured in the frame in which it is at rest
questions.explanation: Proper length is measured by an observer at rest relative to the object. Observers moving relative to it measure a shorter length along the direction of motion, so the proper length is the longest length measured.

questions.stem: A spaceship moves past Earth at 0.8c. The crew measure their ship's length, and an observer on Earth also measures it. Which statement is correct?
options: Both measure the same length, because length is the same in all frames
The crew measure a longer length than the proper length
The crew measure the proper length; the Earth observer measures a shorter length
The Earth observer measures the proper length; the crew measure a shorter length
questions.explanation: The crew are at rest relative to the ship, so they measure its proper length. The Earth observer sees the ship moving at 0.8c and measures it contracted along its motion. The crew would, in turn, measure distances on Earth along the line of motion as contracted.

questions.stem: What is the greatest speed that any object with mass can reach?
options: Any speed, given enough energy
Twice the speed of light in a vacuum
Less than the speed of light in a vacuum
Exactly the speed of light in a vacuum
questions.explanation: An object with mass can approach c but never reach it, because its momentum and energy would have to become infinite. Only massless particles such as photons travel at exactly c.

questions.stem: Why can no amount of energy accelerate a particle with mass up to the speed of light?
options: Energy stops being converted to motion once a particle reaches 0.5c
Its relativistic momentum increases without limit as its speed approaches c
Its mass decreases to zero as its speed approaches c
The air in the accelerator slows it down more and more as it speeds up
questions.explanation: Relativistic momentum grows faster and faster as v approaches c, tending to infinity, so reaching c would need infinite energy. Particle accelerators are evacuated, so air is not the reason.

questions.stem: A constant force acts on an electron for a very long time. How do its momentum and speed change, according to special relativity?
options: Its momentum increases steadily, while its speed approaches c but never reaches it
Its momentum and its speed both increase steadily without limit
Its speed increases steadily, while its momentum levels off at a maximum
Both its momentum and its speed stop increasing once it nears c
questions.explanation: A constant force changes momentum at a constant rate, so momentum keeps increasing. But relativistic momentum rises steeply near c, so the speed creeps closer to c without ever reaching it. Newtonian physics would predict the speed rising steadily past c.

questions.stem: A particle moves at 0.9c. How does its relativistic momentum compare with the Newtonian value mv?
options: It is equal to mv
It is zero, because the particle is close to c
It is greater than mv
It is less than mv
questions.explanation: Relativistic momentum is always greater than mv, and the difference grows as v approaches c. At 0.9c it is already more than twice the Newtonian value. At everyday speeds the two are almost exactly equal.

questions.stem: What does mass-energy equivalence, E = mc², mean?
options: An object's energy is always equal to its kinetic energy
Mass is a form of energy, so a change in mass means a change in energy
Mass increases as the square of an object's speed
Energy can only be produced by converting mass into light and heat
questions.explanation: Einstein's result, from special relativity, is that mass and energy are equivalent: an object at rest has rest energy mc², and losing a mass m releases energy mc². It applies to all energy changes, not only those producing light.

questions.stem: When a uranium-235 nucleus undergoes fission, the total mass of the products is slightly less than the total mass of the reactants. What does this show?
options: Neutrons escaped from the reaction without being counted
The missing mass has been released as energy, in line with E = mc²
Some of the mass has been destroyed without any energy released
The products are moving too fast for their mass to be measured
questions.explanation: Mass-energy equivalence explains the energy released in nuclear reactions: the decrease in mass, the mass defect, appears as the kinetic energy of the products and as radiation. Mass and energy together are conserved.

questions.stem: Why do nuclear reactions release far more energy per kilogram of fuel than chemical reactions such as burning?
options: A larger fraction of the mass is converted, and c² makes even tiny mass changes give huge energies
Nuclear reactions convert all of their fuel's mass into energy, while chemical reactions convert none
Nuclear fuels are denser, so a kilogram of them contains more atoms than a kilogram of coal
Chemical reactions absorb energy, while nuclear reactions always release it
questions.explanation: c² is about 9 × 10¹⁶ m² s⁻², so a tiny mass change gives a large energy. Nuclear reactions convert a much larger fraction of the mass than chemical reactions do, though still well under 1%. Neither kind converts all of the mass.

questions.stem: The Sun radiates enormous amounts of energy. What does mass-energy equivalence tell us about the Sun?
options: It is gaining mass, as the energy it produces in its core turns into new matter
Its mass stays exactly constant, because energy is conserved
It is losing mass only because the solar wind carries particles away
It is losing mass, as fusion converts mass into the energy it radiates
questions.explanation: In the Sun's core, fusion produces nuclei whose total mass is slightly less than that of the reacting nuclei, and the difference leaves as radiation. The Sun therefore loses mass continually as it shines. The solar wind removes mass too, but that is not the source of its energy.

questions.stem: In what year did Einstein publish his special theory of relativity?
questions.explanation: Einstein published special relativity in 1905, the same year as his paper showing that mass and energy are equivalent. His general theory of relativity, which deals with gravity, followed in 1915.
